name: Sodium bicarbonate
short: Most common side-effects by mouth: bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. A case report of excessive intake lists metabolic alkalosis, low potassium and gastric rupture among the risks.
text: A sports nutrition position stand reports that the most common side-effects of sodium bicarbonate taken by mouth are bloating, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; their incidence and severity vary between and within individuals but are generally low, and single doses of 0.4 or 0.5 g/kg were associated with more frequent and more severe side-effects than 0.3 g/kg. Serious harm from excessive intake is described in a case report: a report of a patient admitted to hospital three times in four months after taking bicarbonate for dyspepsia lists the risks of acute and chronic oral intake as including metabolic alkalosis, high blood sodium, hypertension, gastric rupture, low potassium and low chloride, and says that abruptly stopping long-term excessive intake may result in high blood potassium, low aldosterone, volume contraction and disrupted calcium and phosphorus metabolism, while noting that little toxicity had been documented despite widespread use. On blood pressure the evidence is two-sided: that report lists hypertension as a risk, whereas a meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (2110 people) of sodium bicarbonate in chronic kidney disease found no effect on systolic blood pressure and no increase in the use of antihypertensive medicines or diuretics. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
